title: risk_coverage(reduce="max") normalises by the ANTI-oracle, not by a random selector, so aurc_excess_max is silently deflated in all 136 published j2a records
defect: For reduce="max", `aurc_random = error.max(dim=-1).values` is the AURC of the worst-possible ordering (descending error makes cummax equal the global max at every coverage, so its mean is exactly error.max()), not the AURC of a random ordering, so `aurc_excess = (aurc - oracle)/(max - oracle)` is normalised against an adversarial reference while the docstring and the key name assert "1 = worthless".
failure_scenario: results/perstructure/j2a/disjoint_test_1200K.pt, error e_maxcomp (n=2139): the code reports aurc_random=3.3330 (= global max) while a 2000-permutation Monte-Carlo estimate of the true random-ordering AURC is 2.9891 and the oracle is 0.7376. The published aurc_excess_max is 0.823 for the primary oracle exact_maxcomp and 0.823 for random_null — identical to three decimals — yet 0.823 reads on the documented scale as "18% of the way from worthless to perfect". Correctly normalised, both are 0.949/0.948, i.e. the primary oracle is ~5% better than random, not ~18%. Across the 24 published (cache x error) cells the random_null control lands at 0.656-0.965 instead of ~1.0, so the scale has no anchor; for comparison the mean-reduce variant, whose aurc_random is correct, puts random_null at 0.984-1.046. Feeding the exact anti-oracle signal (-error) returns aurc_excess = 1.000000 exactly, confirming the denominator is the worst-case, not the random-case, reference.
evidence: Ran risk_coverage(reduce="max") on all 10 per-structure caches and compared its aurc_random against a 2000-permutation MC estimate of E[mean_k cummax(error[perm])[k]]; also read results/records/j2a_oracle_panel.jsonl and tabulated aurc_excess_max for random_null vs exact_maxcomp/exact_global/force_norm.

title: auprc has no tie handling: a fully tied (degenerate) signal can score 0.68 average precision when the true value is 0.20
defect: `signal.argsort(dim=-1, descending=True)` breaks ties by an arbitrary (unstable, backend-dependent) permutation and the running precision is then accumulated within tie groups, so average precision depends on input index order instead of on the score — unlike `_rank`/`auroc` in the same module, whose docstrings make exact tie handling an explicit design requirement.
failure_scenario: signal = torch.zeros(20) (a completely worthless constant signal), positive = 4 True entries. With the positives at indices 16-19 the function returns auprc = 0.6792; with the same signal and the positives at indices 0-3 it returns 0.1400. The tie-correct (sklearn-convention, step over distinct thresholds) answer is 0.2000 in both cases — an error of up to +0.48. This is latent for the current point estimates (I checked: no exact ties exist in any signal or error tensor in results/perstructure/j2a/*.pt), but it becomes live the moment auprc is used the way the module docstring advertises — inside a bootstrap, where resampling with replacement guarantees duplicate structures and hence exact ties. Bootstrapping auprc on water-disjoint_pimd_T300K with the project's own moving_block_indices(n=500, 400 reps, block_len=3) gives mean 0.5932 vs a tie-correct 0.6032 (-0.010 bias), with 184 of 400 replicates off by more than 0.01 and a worst-case replicate error of 0.033.
evidence: Wrote a float64 tie-correct AP reference (step over distinct thresholds); it agrees with auprc to 2.2e-16 on 200 untied cases but disagrees on 286/300 heavy-tie cases with max error 0.75. Also ran the bootstrap comparison on the real water cache. Note J2A_ORACLE_PANEL.md line 33 claims auprc was "verified ... against a hand-computed average-precision example" — the example evidently contained no ties.

title: risk_coverage's aurc_excess is order-dependent for a tied signal: a worthless constant signal scores 0.0 (perfect) or 2.57 depending on input index order
defect: `_curve` orders by `key.argsort(dim=-1)` with no tie handling, so when the signal has ties the selective-risk curve is decided by array index order rather than by the signal, and the same worthless signal can be reported as a perfect or a worse-than-random selector.
failure_scenario: error = [1., 2., 3., 4., 100.], signal = zeros(5): risk_coverage returns aurc_excess = 0.0, i.e. indistinguishable from the oracle, for a constant (zero-information) signal. Flip the error array to [100., 4., 3., 2., 1.] with the same constant signal and it returns 2.567. The correct value for a signal carrying no information is 1.0 in both cases. Reachable whenever a screening signal is quantised or gated (many exact zeros/clipped values) or inside a bootstrap where resampling duplicates structures.
evidence: Direct call to risk_coverage with a constant signal and the two error orderings; the mean-reduce curve was separately validated against a float64 numpy reference (max err 2.2e-16) on untied inputs.

title: auroc returns 0.0 — a real, plausible-looking AUROC — for positive sets where AUROC is undefined, including the NaN-error path
defect: `(n_pos * n_neg).clamp(min=1)` converts the undefined cases n_pos=0 and n_pos=n into a finite 0.0 instead of NaN, so a degenerate positive set is indistinguishable from a perfectly anti-correlated signal.
failure_scenario: auroc(signal=[0.1,0.9,0.5,0.3], positive=all-False) returns 0.0, and auroc(same signal, positive=all-True) also returns 0.0; both are undefined. This is reachable through top_p_mask (tail_metrics.py:64-65): a single NaN in the error vector makes `error.sort(descending=True)` put NaN first, so for k<=1 the threshold is NaN and `error >= NaN` is False everywhere — top_p_mask(torch.tensor([1.,2.,nan,4.]), 0.25) returns an all-False mask (n_pos=0), and the subsequent auroc call returns 0.0 rather than raising or returning NaN. Inside paired_bootstrap that 0.0 would enter the replicate distribution and drag the lower CI bound down without any diagnostic.
evidence: Direct calls to auroc and top_p_mask with degenerate/NaN inputs; also confirmed _rank ranks NaN as the largest value (scipy returns all-NaN for the same input), so NaN in the signal instead of the error silently yields AUROC = 1.0 for a NaN-carrying positive.

title: risk_coverage's denominator clamp turns an undefined 0/0 normalisation into ~1e27 instead of NaN
defect: `denom = (aurc_random - aurc_oracle).clamp(min=1e-30)` guards the sign of the denominator but not its scale, so when the error distribution is near-degenerate (aurc_random rounds equal to aurc_oracle) the nonzero numerator is divided by 1e-30 and the function returns an astronomically large number for a quantity documented to lie in [0, 1].
failure_scenario: float32 error = [97013.78125, 97013.7890625, 97013.7890625] with signal = [0.6967, 0.633, 0.16]: risk_coverage returns aurc = 97013.7890625, aurc_oracle = aurc_random = 97013.78125, aurc_excess = 7.8125e+27. The same inputs promoted to float64 give aurc_excess = 1.8. A second seeded case (n=4, errors within 2 ULP of 31953.53) gives 1.95e+27 against a float64 answer of 1.54. The current call site (experiments/j2a_oracle_panel.py:108) casts to float64 so this is latent, but risk_coverage carries no dtype guard and would write the garbage straight into a JSON record.
evidence: Randomised float32 search over near-constant error vectors (200k trials, torch seed 20260902) found blow-ups within a few thousand trials; three cases reproduced deterministically and cross-checked against the float64 result.

title: autocorr_function maps a NaN or inf series to all-zero autocorrelation, so integrated_autocorr_time reports the series as independent instead of failing
defect: `return acf / acf[0] if acf[0] > 0 else np.zeros_like(acf)` treats NaN (for which `acf[0] > 0` is False) exactly like a constant series, so a corrupted input silently produces rho = 0 everywhere.
failure_scenario: x = a 500-step random walk with x[10] = np.nan: integrated_autocorr_time returns {'tau_int': 1.0, 'window': 5, 'rho_1': 0.0, 'time_ordered': False} — the exact signature the module docstring designates as "the ordering was not meaningful". The clean series returns tau_int = 29.17, rho_1 = 0.976, time_ordered = True. np.inf gives the same false-negative. Because experiments/j1_build_splits.py:45 and j9a_leading_only_ci.py:96 feed this straight into block_length(), a corrupted error series would yield block_len = 2 and silently collapse the moving-block bootstrap into an IID bootstrap (bootstrap_block.py:33 short-circuits to iid_indices for block_len <= 1) and shrink the split guard band to 2, with no warning and no NaN anywhere in the recorded diagnostics.
evidence: Called integrated_autocorr_time on a random walk with one NaN and with one inf, versus the clean series; only numpy RuntimeWarnings are emitted, and the returned dict is fully finite and self-consistent.

title: Reported 95% bootstrap CIs exclude 19/20 alternative split draws of the same quantity
defect: The paired block bootstrap resamples only the test structures while holding the single design/cal/test split draw fixed, so the interval it reports omits the dominant source of variation in the quantity it is presented as an interval for.
failure_scenario: Re-run the exact L=5 pipeline (lo_r0=4, cv_r0=2, cv_K=4, alpha=0.05, 10 frozen probe seeds) on rMD17 ethanol with contiguous_block_split(n=1000, tau_int=1.179, guard=3) under 20 alternative split seeds instead of 20260901. Shipped seed gives delta = +0.078 with the published CI [+0.062, +0.093] (J2B_FACTOR_B.md, 'With paired block-bootstrap intervals'); the 20 alternative draws give +0.084 .. +0.131 (mean +0.111, sd 0.014), so 19 of 20 lie outside the published 95% interval. 3BPA disjoint: published [+0.013,+0.029], alternatives +0.005..+0.050, 8/20 outside. 3BPA overlapping: published [-0.009,-0.002], alternatives -0.014..-0.003, 8/20 outside. The point estimates in J2B_FACTOR_B.md section 3 move even more: ethanol leading-only skip fraction is published as 0.724 (L=3) but ranges 0.453-0.784 (sd 0.082) across the 24 other split seeds I tried; 3BPA disjoint 0.813 published, 0.640-0.825 across seeds. The sign of the LO-CV difference is robust (20/20 same sign on all three systems), so the qualitative claim survives, but every interval and every 'significant' flag understates uncertainty by roughly a factor of two to four.
evidence: Script /tmp/claude-69101/.../scratchpad/s7.py and s6.py, run with PYTHONPATH=src under the fs-cpu python, reusing acquisition/conformal_c/est_cv/est_leading_only from experiments/j2b_factor_b.py and leading_head_directions from the frozen tree; the shipped-seed reproduction reproduces the published deltas exactly (+0.021 / +0.078 / -0.005), so only the split seed varies.

title: coverage_law's Beta(k, n+1-k) band is quoted for the blocked split, where it understates realised spread by ~70%
defect: Beta(k, n_cal+1-k) is exact only when the calibration scores and the test score are exchangeable, but j1_build_splits.py:59 evaluates it on the contiguous_block split, whose calibration role is one contiguous window of an autocorrelated trajectory, and the resulting band is published as the paper's 'Calibration power' table.
failure_scenario: Simulate n=2139 with an AR(1) nonconformity ratio at tau_int = 4.0 (3BPA disjoint's measured 3.96), apply contiguous_block_split(seed=20260901, guard=8) -> n_cal=412, take c_alpha as the ceil((n+1)*0.95)-th order statistic on cal and measure coverage on test, 3000 replicates. Realised coverage: mean 0.9495, sd 0.0179, 90% band [0.9166, 0.9754]. coverage_law(412, 0.05) claims sd 0.0106 and [0.9331, 0.9676] -- exactly the '0.950 [0.932, 0.968]' printed for 3BPA in results/J1_SPLIT_REPAIR.md. Realised P(coverage < 0.90) is 0.011 against the Beta law's 4.65e-5, a factor of 240. On random_frame_split with the same data the law is accurate (realised sd 0.0120 vs law 0.0104), which isolates the contiguous calibration window as the cause. Consistent with this, measured test-split coverage of the shipped leading_only gate over the 10 real caches is 0.946 mean under contiguous_block (6/10 below nominal, min 0.924) versus 0.964 under random_frame (2/10 below, min 0.942).
evidence: Scripts /tmp/claude-69101/.../scratchpad/s5.py (simulation) and s4.py (real-cache gate coverage, using experiments/j2b_factor_b.conformal_c and the shipped manifests).

title: contiguous_block_split's documented anti-confound safeguard does not occur: calibration is one contiguous window and every test frame precedes every calibration frame
defect: The block-to-role permutation depends only on (seed, n_blocks) and not on the system, so all ten manifests share one layout, and for the shipped seed that layout is T D T T T T T C C D -- both calibration blocks adjacent -- which is precisely the drift/role confound the docstring at lines 78-82 says the permutation prevents.
failure_scenario: np.random.default_rng(20260901).permutation(10) applied to ['design','design','cal','cal','test'*6] yields role layout ['T','D','T','T','T','T','T','C','C','D']. In all 10 shipped manifests/splits/*__contiguous_block.json the cal role is a single contiguous run (cal_contiguous=True everywhere) occupying frames ~0.70n-0.90n, and max(test index) < min(cal index) in every one (e.g. disjoint_test_1200K test [0,1488], cal [1505,1916]; rmd17-disjoint_ethanol test [0,696], cal [703,896]; water-disjoint_md_T300K test [0,345], cal [354,445]). So c_alpha is calibrated on a strictly later 20% window of the trajectory than the entire test set it is applied to, for every system, and the split-conformal exchangeability premise holds only if the trajectory has no drift at all. A KS test of the cal-vs-test nonconformity ratios does not reject on these particular caches (p = 0.13-0.97), so the flaw is latent here rather than actively biasing the published numbers -- but it is the mechanism behind the split-seed sensitivity above, and the docstring asserts a protection the code does not deliver.
evidence: Scripts /tmp/claude-69101/.../scratchpad/s3.py, s6.py (layout + run structure), s11.py (KS test on real caches). The contiguous-run decomposition of each role was read directly from the shipped manifests.

title: Percentile block-bootstrap intervals labelled 95% attain ~90% coverage at the project's own block-length rule
defect: paired_difference/paired_bootstrap emit a plain percentile interval at nominal alpha and a boolean `significant` flag, but with block_len = ceil(2*tau_int) (autocorr.py:69) the interval attains only ~0.90 coverage when tau_int is materially above 1, so `significant` is a ~10%-level test rather than the 5% one every table treats it as.
failure_scenario: AR(1) with phi=0.6 (tau_int = 4.0, the value measured for 3BPA disjoint), statistic = sample mean, 1500 replicates, n_boot=400, block_len taken from block_length(integrated_autocorr_time(x)): coverage of the nominal-95% interval is 0.913 at n=1259, 0.903 at n=500, 0.905 at n=2139 (MC se 0.008); doubling the block gives 0.922-0.928 and quadrupling 0.918-0.933, so the deficit is the block-length rule plus the un-studentised percentile method, not Monte-Carlo noise. iid scheme on the same draws covers 0.67-0.69. Concretely: a paired_difference call on a tau_int=4 series that reports ci_lo=+0.001, ci_hi=+0.060 and significant=True is being read as a 5% test but its true type-I rate is ~10%. results/J1_SPLIT_REPAIR.md already records the 89.0% measurement, but nothing downstream adjusts -- every record still writes ci_lo/ci_hi at alpha=0.05 and J2A/J2B count '19/24 significant' and '5 of 6 systems' at face value.
evidence: Scripts /tmp/claude-69101/.../scratchpad/s2.py, s9.py, s10.py calling the shipped paired_bootstrap directly. moving_block_indices itself is correct -- I verified circular contiguity within blocks and uniform marginals (0.0098-0.0100 against a 0.0099 target over 20000 draws at n=101, b=7) -- so the defect is the block-length rule and the interval type, not the resampler.

title: conformal_c silently clamps the order-statistic index instead of returning +inf when alpha is infeasible for n_cal
defect: `k = min(n, max(1, ceil((n+1)*(1-alpha))))` clamps to the maximum observed ratio when ceil((n+1)(1-alpha)) > n_cal, producing an anti-conservative gate, and splits.alpha_feasible -- which exists to catch exactly this and mandates recording the cell as `underpowered` -- is never called anywhere outside tests/test_splits.py.
failure_scenario: Run j2b_factor_b.py --alpha 0.01 on any water cache: n_cal is 92-94, so alpha_feasible(92, 0.01) = (False, k=93) and coverage_law returns {'feasible': False}, but conformal_c clamps k to 92 and returns a finite c_alpha; the emitted record carries "alpha": 0.01 with no feasibility field and the gate is reported as a valid 99% gate. Measured on exchangeable Uniform(0,1) ratios, 20000 trials: n_cal=50/alpha=0.01 gives 0.9800 coverage against nominal 0.99; n_cal=15/alpha=0.05 gives 0.9379 against nominal 0.95; n_cal=92/alpha=0.01 gives 0.9895. All shipped records use alpha=0.05 where every n_cal (92-428) is feasible, so no published number is affected -- this is latent. grep confirms `alpha_feasible(` appears in no experiment: j1_build_splits.py imports it at line 26 and never calls it, and no record in results/records/*.jsonl carries a feasible/underpowered field.
evidence: Script /tmp/claude-69101/.../scratchpad/s8.py section A, calling the shipped conformal_c and alpha_feasible; grep -n 'alpha_feasible(' over experiments/ returns nothing outside the import line.

title: paired_bootstrap/paired_difference default to scheme="block" with block_len=1, silently performing an IID bootstrap while recording scheme="block"
defect: The default arguments are scheme="block", block_len=1, and moving_block_indices short-circuits to iid_indices for block_len <= 1, so a caller that supplies the scheme but forgets the block length gets the IID resampler with a record that claims the block scheme.
failure_scenario: paired_difference(auroc, sig_a, sig_b, pos) on a trajectory with tau_int = 4 returns {"scheme": "block", "block_len": 1, ...} while having run the IID bootstrap, whose coverage on that data I measured at 0.67-0.69 against the nominal 0.95. An auditor reading the record's scheme field concludes the autocorrelation-robust scheme was used. The block_len field does expose it, but the scheme field contradicts it, and the module docstring's entire argument is that the IID scheme is invalid for trajectory data. The shipped j2a/j5 CI records do carry block_len 2/3/5, so no published number is affected.
evidence: Read of bootstrap_block.py lines 33-34 and 47-48/78-79; confirmed by calling paired_bootstrap(mean_metric, x, scheme="block") with defaults and observing identical indices to iid_indices under the same generator seed.

title: beta_noise's `shared` branch is distributionally identical to `indep`, so J3's "coordinate coupling is irrelevant" conclusion rests on a comparison with zero power
defect: The `shared=True` branch draws each coordinate's head-space direction `A[s,d,:]` independently and isotropically, so conditional on the shared frame `O` the D projection fractions are i.i.d. Beta(K/2,(r-K)/2) and independent of O — mathematically the exact same law as the `shared=False` branch — meaning the shared random subspace induces no coordinate coupling whatsoever and the two arms cannot differ except by Monte-Carlo noise.
failure_scenario: Run `beta_noise(v, r=7, K=4, shared=True)` and `shared=False` on any v: both return i.i.d. Beta(2, 1.5) fractions. Because the whole point of Step 2 is that `shared` is "what the real estimator does" and `indep` is "the marginal model", J3_EXTREME_VALUE.md's bolded conclusion **"Coordinate coupling is irrelevant... shared and indep agree to within ~0.02"** is an artefact: it is reporting agreement between two draws from one distribution. The real estimator does have coupling, so the simulation is also silently mis-specified in the direction the doc attributes to an unexplained "+0.03 optimism".
evidence: (1) Equivalence: on v=ones(4000,81), r=7, K=4 the two branches give mean/var 0.5710/0.05450 vs 0.5717/0.05442 (Beta analytic 0.5714/0.05442), two-sample KS on 100k values p=0.38; mean cross-coordinate correlation of `frac` is 0.00012 (shared) vs 0.00015 (indep). (2) Zero power: rerunning Step 2 on head_forces_disjoint_test_1200K.pt with n_rep=200 instead of 10 gives shared-minus-indep = -0.0036 / +0.0053 / -0.0017 at K=3/4/6, i.e. ~0; the per-replicate sd is 0.030-0.040 so the SE of each arm at the shipped n_rep=10 is ~0.011, which fully accounts for the 0.018-0.034 differences the shipped record shows (e.g. same_test_1200K K=4: 0.656 vs 0.622; ethanol K=6: 0.744 vs 0.714). (3) Mis-specification: the real Haar estimator on the same cache has mean cross-coordinate correlation of v_hat/v equal to 0.035, ~300x the simulation's 0.0001; consequently the across-structure sd of the within-structure mean of v_hat/v is 0.0506 measured vs 0.0259 for i.i.d. Beta (sqrt(0.0544/81)) — the simulation understates the structure-level noise by 2x. (4) `M = r + 1` and `Qc = helmert_basis(M, ...)` on lines 92-93 are computed and never used, i.e. the intended construction (route the directions through the same centred basis the estimator uses) was left unfinished. (5) Rerunning the script reproduces results/records/j3_extreme_value.json byte-identically, so this is the code that produced the published table.

title: risk_coverage(reduce="max") normalises by the global max instead of the expected random-ordering AURC, so `aurc_excess_max` is deflated ~10% and its documented "1 = worthless" scale is false
defect: For `reduce="max"` the random reference is set to `error.max()`, but the expected AURC of a genuinely random acceptance ordering under a running-max curve is the mean over coverage of E[max of the first k], which is strictly below the global max; the denominator is therefore too large and every signal's `aurc_excess_max` is pulled toward 0 (i.e. toward "oracle").
failure_scenario: j2a_oracle_panel.py:111 stores `aurc_excess_max` for all 232 records under a docstring that states the scale is "0 = perfect, 1 = worthless". Feed it the `random_null` signal (a worthless signal by construction) on head_forces_disjoint_test_1200K.pt and it returns 0.933, not 1.0; on rmd17-disjoint_azobenzene it returns 0.736. A reader comparing exact_global's 0.70 against a nominal worthless value of 1.0 concludes the signal recovers 30% of the oracle gap on the safety-relevant worst-case metric, when the correctly normalised figure is 22%.
evidence: On head_forces_disjoint_test_1200K.pt with e_max: aurc(random null)=3.3744, aurc_oracle=0.8677, aurc_random as coded (global max)=3.5531, but E[AURC_max] over 300 random permutations = 3.2768. Correctly normalised, the random null scores 1.041 (as it should) versus the 0.933 the code reports; exact_global scores 0.781 correctly versus the 0.701 stored in the records. The bias grows with n and with tail heaviness. The `reduce="mean"` branch is correct (random null gives 0.958-1.027 across all ten caches), which is why the error is invisible in the metric that the docs actually quote.

title: j9a fixes the control variate at cv_r0=2 for every lane budget while leading-only gets r0 = lanes-1, inflating the reported skip-fraction advantage by up to 2.6x
defect: `--cv-r0` defaults to 2 and is never scaled with `--lanes`, so the "matched budget" head-to-head compares a leading-only estimator whose rank is tuned to the budget against a control variate whose exact-subspace rank is frozen at 2 — even though r0 is fitted on the design split and is therefore free to be chosen per budget under the same split discipline.
failure_scenario: At L=6 on rMD17 ethanol, j9a reports skip_lo=0.941, skip_cv=0.894, delta=+0.047 [+0.034,+0.061]. Run the same 6-lane budget with the control variate's own design-fitted r0=4 (K=5) and its skip fraction is 0.9227, so the true matched-budget margin is +0.018 — 2.6x smaller than the published interval, whose lower bound (+0.034) excludes it. The sign is preserved on every system, but the effect sizes quoted in J2B_FACTOR_B.md ("+0.014 to +0.158") are systematically overstated at the larger budgets.
evidence: j2b's own sweep records already contain the better configuration: sweep_global_r04.jsonl has control_variate K=5, r0=4, uq_lanes=6, 10 seeds, mean frac_exact_skipped=0.9227, while sweepcv_global_K5.jsonl has control_variate K=5, r0=2, uq_lanes=6, mean 0.8936 — same total lane budget. Same pattern on aspirin at 7 lanes (CV r0=5: 0.912 vs CV r0=2: 0.885) and azobenzene at 7 lanes (0.899 vs 0.866). Verified LO/CV lane accounting matches: leading_only uq_lanes = r0+1, control_variate uq_lanes = K+1.

title: j9a's output filename omits the cache set, so a water run silently overwrote the record backing the published L=5 table
defect: The output path is keyed only on `--score` and `--lanes`, not on `--cache-dirs`, and there is no `--out` override, so two runs at the same lane budget over different system sets collide on one filename and the later run destroys the earlier record.
failure_scenario: Running `j9a_leading_only_ci.py --lanes 5` on the frozen caches and then again with `--cache-dirs results/processed` (water) leaves only the water rows. That has already happened: results/records/j9a_leading_only_ci_global_L5.json contains exactly ['water-disjoint_md_T300K','water-disjoint_pimd_T300K','water-overlapping_md_T300K','water-overlapping_pimd_T300K'], while J2B_FACTOR_B.md's L=5 CI column publishes the six frozen systems (3BPA disjoint +0.021 [+0.013,+0.029], ethanol +0.078 [+0.062,+0.093], ...). No record file in results/records/ contains those six L=5 rows, so a published table has no surviving machine-readable provenance.
evidence: Listed the `system` field of each j9a record: L4 and L6 hold the six frozen systems, L5 holds only the four water systems. Re-running `--score global --lanes 5` on the default (frozen) cache dir reproduces the doc's six L=5 rows exactly (0.929/0.909/+0.021 [+0.013,+0.029] for disjoint_test_1200K, etc.) and rewrites the same path, confirming the collision.

title: The `lanes=8` cell silently ran only 7 lanes in every J8 benchmark on every GPU
defect: `exact_seed_bundle(M, B).seeds` has shape [M-1, B, M] = [7, B, 8] for this M=8 committee, so `.seeds[:L]` silently returns 7 rows for L=8 (Python slicing does not error on an over-long slice), meaning every cell recorded as `lanes: 8` measured a 7-lane VJP.
failure_scenario: Inputs: the 3BPA/water MACE committee (M=8, recorded as `"M": 8` in every record) and `--lanes 1 2 3 4 8`. Wrong output: 48 records across five jsonl files carry `"lanes": 8` with a 7-lane timing. Downstream, (a) every least-squares fit places a 7-lane measurement at x=8, biasing every published slope low by exactly the OLS factor 24.8/29.2 = 0.849 -- 3BPA serial 10.92 -> 12.86 ms/lane, 3BPA batched B=64 8.08 -> 9.48, water B=16 batched 49.76 -> 58.57, water B=32 serial 94.27 -> 110.99, and the derived constants 0.0196 / 0.026 ms per (edge/SM) per lane -> 0.0231 / 0.0306; (b) every 'exact (L=8)' entry is short by one lane (the LaneBudget for exact is 7 UQ + 1 mean = 8), so the R5 speedup table understates itself: 3BPA B=64 1.58x -> 1.77x, water B=16 1.63x -> 1.84x, water B=32 1.65x -> 1.86x, and the 5-lane gate 1.38x -> 1.49x (3BPA B=64), 1.41x -> 1.52x (water B=16).
evidence: Ran `exact_seed_bundle(8, 4, dtype=torch.float32)`: seeds.shape = (7, 4, 8), K = 7, LaneBudget(uq_lanes=7, mean_lanes=1); `seeds[:8].shape[0] == 7` while `seeds[:7].shape[0] == 7`. Ran j8_lane_bench.py myself on an available A100 MIG slice with `--lanes 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8`: at B=64 batched the L->L+1 increments are 23.94, 24.85, 25.98, 25.34, 25.78, 25.95 and then **-0.35** for 7->8 (T(7)=212.25 vs T(8)=211.90); same at B=64 serial (201.58 vs 200.48) and B=1 serial (156.32 vs 157.60). The signature is already present in the published records: (T8-T4)/(T4-T3) = 3.00 +/- 0.15 across all 25 lane-proportional cells on three GPUs (3BPA A100 [3.00,3.24,3.00,3.16,3.04,3.16,2.92,3.01]; water [2.95,2.90,3.36,2.62,2.82,2.97,3.00,3.07,2.99,3.02]; Blackwell [2.97,3.85,2.97,2.89,2.92,2.99,2.76]) where 4.00 is required if 8 lanes had run. Refitting every cell with the L=8 point relabelled x=7 raises R^2 from 0.988-0.994 to 0.9995-1.0000 and multiplies every slope by 1/0.849 (observed ratios 0.848-0.853 in every lane-proportional cell). The frozen workshop script scripts/02b_lane_scaling.py:102 builds seeds as `torch.randn(L, B, M)` and does run 8 real lanes (its docstring: 'Exact force UQ needs L = M = 8 (one mean lane + M-1 centered directions)'), so the journal rewrite introduced the regression and J8_SMOKE_A100.md:22's 'agrees with the laptop's [11.78] to within 8%' compares a 15%-biased slope with an unbiased one.

title: The verdict script loads the pre-registered protocol and never uses it; all thresholds and admission conditions are Python literals
defect: `proto = yaml.safe_load(...)` (line 46) and `T = load(THREEBPA)` (line 45) are dead: every prediction threshold, the lane set, the batch set, the iteration counts and the hardware condition are hardcoded in Python, and the 3BPA reference figures on lines 64-65 are a literal string, so the script cannot detect any divergence between the records it scores and the protocol it claims to score them against.
failure_scenario: Input: rewrite protocols/j8_water_prediction.yaml so P1 reads 'exceeds 500 ms/lane', P2 '>= 9.0x', P3 'transition occurs at B >= 1000', P4 'serial slope is BELOW 1 ms/lane', primary_metric a fit over L in {1..8}, config {iters: 5000, dtype: float64, batch_sizes: [999], lanes: [7]}, hardware 'H200, MIG required'. Wrong output: byte-identical run, still 'VERDICT: 4/4 pre-registered predictions confirmed'. Same output when the file is replaced with `nothing: here`. Concretely this let a MIG-slice record -- which j8_lane_bench.py:115 itself flags '*** WARNING: MIG device. Timings are NOT publishable. ***', with lanes {1,2,4,8} instead of the pre-registered {1,2,3,4,8} and iters=20/warmup=10 instead of 50/25 -- be scored '4/4 confirmed'.
evidence: grep shows `proto` appears only at line 46 and inside string literals; `T` only at line 45. Ran the script from a scratchpad copy against the mutated and the stubbed YAML: identical output both times. Re-ran it with results/records/j8_water_verdict_source_MIG.jsonl in place of the water record: it printed 4/4 PASS and reproduced results/records/j8_water_verdict_MIG.json exactly (speedup_B16 = 1.627743062173085, transition_batch = 1) -- the run J8_WATER_VERDICT.md:10-11 cites as independent corroboration. The output JSON records no provenance at all (no device_name, is_mig, source path, iters), and both the MIG and A100 verdicts are written to the same fixed filename results/records/j8_water_verdict.json.

title: `fit()` silently drops OOM cells and accepts 2-point fits, so the pre-registered primary metric can be scored off a truncated lane set
defect: The fit filters on `status == "ok"` and only requires `len(pts) >= 2`, so an OOM at the largest L -- always the highest-leverage point -- removes it from the least-squares fit without changing the reported quantity, the printed table (which shows no n) or the pass/fail, even though protocols/j8_water_prediction.yaml declares the primary metric to be 'a least-squares fit over L in {1,2,3,4,8}'.
failure_scenario: Input: results/records/j8_water_verdict_source_MIG.jsonl, whose B=16/L=8/batched cell OOM'd ('Tried to allocate 9.15 GiB'). Wrong output: the B=16 batched fit is computed from L in {1,2,4} only (n=3, r2=1.0000 by near-construction) and P1 -- the protocol's falsification clause -- is printed 'measured: 149.59 ms/lane -> PASS' with no indication the primary metric was not evaluated as specified. The sensitivity is decisive, not cosmetic: dropping the L=8 point from the accepted A100 water record flips the B=1 batched slope from +1.33 to -0.05 ms/lane (sign flip, 27x magnitude) and B=2 from 2.49 to 0.54, i.e. it flips both P1's and P3's criterion in the cells that carry them.
evidence: Reproduced results/records/j8_water_verdict_MIG.json exactly; its B=16 batched entry is `"slope": 149.59, "n": 3, "r2": 0.99996` while every other entry has n=4. Recomputed the accepted water fits with and without L=8: B=1 batched 1.33 -> -0.05, B=2 2.49 -> 0.54, B=4 11.23 -> 9.19. The OOM record also lacks peak_alloc_bytes/peak_reserved_bytes (set difference against an ok record: iqr_ms, iters, median_ms, min_ms, peak_alloc_bytes, peak_reserved_bytes, warmup), contradicting j8_lane_bench.py's docstring lines 15-17 that 'the memory boundary appears in the data instead of as a gap'.

title: P3's pass/fail tests only the weak half of the pre-registered statement; the quantified half fails under the script's own rule
defect: Protocol P3 states 'the transition occurs at B <= 4, i.e. at roughly 1/16 to 1/33 of 3BPA's transition batch size, tracking edges rather than structures', but the script tests only `trans <= 4` and never computes 3BPA's transition batch under the same rule (the 3BPA record is loaded and discarded), so the quantified clause is unscored.
failure_scenario: Applying the script's own criterion (first B whose batched slope exceeds 1 ms/lane) to results/records/j8_lane_bench_NVIDIA_A100-SXM4-80GB.jsonl gives 3BPA transition = B 64 (slopes 0.52, 0.51, 0.57, 8.08); water gives B 1. The ratio is 64x, outside the pre-registered 16-33x band, yet P3 prints PASS. J8_WATER_VERDICT.md:52-55 instead quotes 'a 16x reduction in the batch size required', which is derived from a different rule entirely (first B at which the R5 speedup reaches ~1.5x, i.e. B=4), so the document silently switches definitions of 'transition batch size' between line 17 (B=1) and line 55 (B=4) and reports the one that lands inside the pre-registered band.
evidence: Computed both transitions from the records with the script's own `fit()` and `> 1.0` rule: 3BPA -> 64, water -> 1, ratio 64.0x. results/records/j8_water_verdict.json records `"transition_batch": 1` while J8_WATER_VERDICT.md:55 claims 16x.

title: The slope that produces `transition_batch: 1` and the paper's ~10^4-edge rule is not statistically distinguishable from the criterion, and no uncertainty is propagated anywhere
defect: `fit()` returns only intercept/slope/r2/n; no standard error is computed, reported or used, and the water B=1 batched slope of 1.33 ms/lane -- the sole basis for '~10^4 total edges is the threshold' -- has a 95% CI of [0.18, 2.47] against a 1 ms/lane criterion, while the underlying data are flat over the whole deployable lane range.
failure_scenario: Input: the five B=1 batched medians 61.24, 61.18, 61.18, 61.08, 70.02 ms at L = 1,2,3,4,8. The path is flat-to-decreasing over L=1..4 (fitted slope -0.05 ms/lane); the entire 1.33 comes from the single L=8 point, which is itself a 7-lane measurement (see the seeds[:L] finding). Wrong output: `transition_batch: 1` in results/records/j8_water_verdict.json, 'first B with slope > 1 is B = 1 -> PASS' for P3, and J8_WATER_VERDICT.md:57-68 promoting 17,150 edges to 'a threshold a practitioner can check against their own system'. Restricting the fit to the lane range the gate actually operates in (L <= 4) moves water's first crossing of 1 ms/lane from B=1 (17,150 edges) to B=4 (68,600 edges), a 4x move in the headline threshold.
evidence: OLS with 3 dof on the B=1 batched cell: slope 1.33, residual s = 1.95 ms, se(b) = 0.36, t = (1.33-1.0)/0.36 = 0.90 (one-sided p ~ 0.21), 95% CI [0.18, 2.47]; R^2 = 0.818 with a systematic convex residual pattern +1.75, +0.36, -0.97, -2.39, +1.25. B=2 is the same shape (R^2 = 0.884). Every other water cell has R^2 >= 0.978. The IQRs on those four flat points are 0.62-1.48 ms while the points span 0.16 ms in total.

title: The water run's dispersion is misreported by up to 10x, and the misstatement is what dismisses co-tenancy
defect: Line 4 states 'IQRs 0.6-1.3 ms i.e. under 1% of medians' and the caveat at line 115 uses 'IQRs are under 1% of medians' to conclude 'co-tenancy cannot alter any conclusion', but the quoted range is read off the B=16 row alone and is false for the record as a whole.
failure_scenario: Input: the 60 cells of results/records/j8_lane_bench_water.jsonl. Actual IQR range is 0.27-7.17 ms and 0.11%-10.70% of the median, with 34 of 60 cells above 1%; median-min reaches 12.9% (B=4 L=2 batched: min 56.09, median 63.35). The worst-dispersion cells (6.9-10.7%: B=8 L=1 serial, B=2 L=1 batched, B=1 L=1/L=2/L=3 serial, B=4 L=1 serial) are exactly the small-B, low-L cells whose 0.1-0.2 ms separations carry the transition/threshold claim, so the dismissal of co-tenancy is unsupported precisely where it is needed. For contrast the exclusive-node 3BPA A100 run has IQR <= 1.15% and median-min <= 1.3% everywhere.
evidence: Computed IQR/median and (median-min)/min over all cells of all three records. Also: the water record's slurm_partition is `gpu_requeue`, not the protocol's 'exclusive node, MIG disabled'; and its `nvidia_smi` field is a single line '575.57.08, 210 MHz, 1593 MHz, 60.64 W, 0x0000000000000001' -- one sample taken at process start with the GPU idle (throttle bit 0x1 = GpuIdle, SM clock at the 210 MHz idle floor), containing no utilisation or process fields, so 'co-tenancy recorded' on line 4 is not backed by anything in the record.

title: The 5-lane gate is the one configuration never measured, and the interpolation used instead over-states its speedup by ~4%
defect: `--lanes` defaults to [1,2,3,4,8] and the pre-registered config repeats that set, so L=5 -- the deployed gate configuration whose speedup is the headline of both result documents -- was never run on any of the three GPUs; T(5) is instead linearly interpolated on the [4,8] interval, which (because the L=8 cell really ran 7 lanes) has a chord slope only 3/4 of the true per-lane cost.
failure_scenario: Inputs: T(4) = 51.47 ms and 'T(8)' = 81.39 ms (3BPA A100 B=64, R5-selected). Interpolated T(5) = 58.95 ms -> published gate speedup 1.38x. I measured L=5 directly: at B=64 batched, T(5) = 160.52 ms against a chord interpolation of 154.36 ms from the same run's T(4) and T(8) -- the interpolation under-estimates T(5) by 4.0% and therefore over-states the gate speedup by 4.0% (1.373x interpolated vs 1.320x measured). The same bias applies to every '5-lane gate' figure published: 3BPA 1.05/1.05/1.05/1.38x and water 1.11/1.35/1.41/1.42x, all of which are reported in tables where every other column is measured.
evidence: Ran j8_lane_bench.py with `--lanes 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8` on an available A100 MIG slice. B=64 batched T(L) = 60.4, 84.4, 109.2, 135.2, 160.5, 186.3, 212.3, 211.9 -- linear with increment ~25.5 ms/lane through L=7, so T(5) sits 4.0% above the chord drawn from T(4) to the (mislabelled) L=8 point. The bias is systematic and present in every published cell: (T8-T4)/4 divided by (T4-T3) = 0.66-0.84 (median 0.75) across all 26 published fits on three GPUs, i.e. the interpolation interval always carries 3 lanes of work priced as 4.

title: P4's scoring rule (mean of serial slopes) appears nowhere in the protocol and its value is an artefact of the batch grid
defect: The script scores P4 as `mean(serial slope over all measured B) > 10.9`, but protocol P4 makes two claims -- 'the serial path remains approximately affine in L' AND 'its slope will be LARGER than 3BPA's ~10.9 ms/lane' -- and specifies no aggregation; the affinity clause is never tested, and averaging is meaningless here because water's serial slope is strongly batch-dependent while the 3BPA constant it is compared against is not.
failure_scenario: Input: water serial slopes 17.26, 17.74, 18.86, 25.40, 47.98, 94.27 ms/lane over B = 1..32 (a 5.5x range), compared against 3BPA's 10.92-11.07 over B = 1..64 (a 1.4% range). Wrong output: 'measured: mean 36.92 ms/lane' presented as the value of a prediction that never mentions a mean; the same script prints 'mean 47.33' when handed the MIG record whose grid stops at B=16, and would print 17.95 if the grid stopped at B=4 -- three different 'measured' values for one pre-registered quantity, differing only by which batch sizes happened to run.
evidence: Ran the script against both record files: the accepted water record prints 'mean 36.92 (range 17.26-94.27)', the MIG record prints 'mean 47.33 (range 11.52-118.22)'. Recomputed partial means from the accepted record: B<=4 gives 17.95, B<=8 gives 19.82, all B gives 36.92.

title: The pre-registered primary metric is measured on the implementation that rule R5 discards at the batch sizes in question
defect: P1 and P3 are defined on the *batched* slope, but for water the R5 rule (fastest correct implementation selected independently per cell) selects *serial* at every lane count for B >= 8, including B=16 where P1 -- the falsification clause -- is evaluated, so the mechanism claim and the deployed cost path are not the same code path.
failure_scenario: Input: the 30 water cells at B in {8,16,32}. Serial beats batched in all 15 of them (e.g. B=16 L=8: serial 438.74 vs batched 457.60; B=32 L=1: 181.97 vs 190.66). Wrong output: P1 reports the batched slope 49.76 ms/lane at B=16 while the R5-selected implementation there has slope 47.98, and J8_WATER_VERDICT.md section 2 derives the paper's transferable '~10^4 edge' rule entirely from batched slopes even though section 3 of the same document concludes 'For water at B >= 8, serial wins.' A reader applying the rule would characterise a code path the paper's own R5 selection rejects. Relatedly, section 3's R5 summary row '2-4 | batched at L>=4, serial at L=1' is wrong: at B=4 batched already wins at L=2 (63.35 vs 80.69) and L=3 (71.19 vs 101.83).
evidence: Built the full R5 winner map from results/records/j8_lane_bench_water.jsonl: batched wins all 5 lanes at B=1; serial only at L=1 for B=2 and B=4 (batched at L=2,3,4,8); serial at all 5 lanes for B=8, 16 and 32.

title: J8 water R5 table quotes a serial baseline (76.7 ms) that appears in no record; the real value is 183.6 ms
defect: The §3 row `| 1 | batched (70.0 vs 76.7) |` reports the B=1, L=8 serial baseline as 76.7 ms, but `j8_lane_bench_water.jsonl` records 183.58 ms for that cell, and no cell in any j8 record has a median within 0.3 ms of 76.7.

evidence: Loaded results/records/j8_lane_bench_water.jsonl and indexed by (batch_size, lanes, impl): (1,8,'serial') median_ms = 183.58, (1,8,'batched') = 70.02. Scanned all four j8_*.jsonl files for any median_ms within 0.3 ms of 76.7 -> zero matches (only 70.02 batched B=1 L=8, and 69.79 from the discarded MIG run).

title: J8 water IQR claim understates dispersion ~10x and is used to dismiss co-tenancy for conclusions resting on 2-5% effects
defect: "IQRs 0.6-1.3 ms i.e. under 1% of medians" (repeated at line 115 as the reason "co-tenancy cannot alter any conclusion") is the range for B in {16,32} only; over the full 60-cell grid the IQR range is 0.274-7.171 ms and 34 of 60 cells exceed 1% of their median, peaking at 10.7%.

The stated caveat certifies that co-tenancy cannot affect that conclusion, while the records show the run-to-run spread is twice the effect being claimed.

title: P3's evidence "first B with slope > 1 is B = 1" is an artifact of the single L=8 point; water is launch-bound at B=1
defect: The 1.33 ms/lane batched slope at B=1 (quoted at line 17 as P3's evidence and at line 62 as the "1.33 at 17,150 edges" crossing point) comes from a 5-point fit with R2 = 0.818 whose L=1..4 medians are 61.24, 61.18, 61.18, 61.08 ms - a slope of -0.05 ms/lane, i.e. perfectly flat.
failure_scenario: Section 2 concludes "Total edges in the batch is the controlling variable ... ~10^4 edges is a threshold a practitioner can check" by pairing 3BPA's crossing bracket [8,320, 33,280 edges] with water's claimed crossing at 17,150 edges. Refitting water over L<=4 gives -0.05 (B=1), +0.54 (B=2), +9.19 (B=4) ms/lane, so water actually crosses 1 ms/lane between 34,300 and 68,600 edges; the two brackets then barely overlap and the ~10^4-edge threshold that §4 sells as the paper's transferable systems rule is unsupported.
evidence: Least-squares fits on j8_lane_bench_water.jsonl batched medians. L in {1,2,3,4,8}: B=1 slope 1.326 (R2 0.818), B=2 2.485 (R2 0.884). L in {1,2,3,4}: B=1 -0.050, B=2 0.541, B=4 9.187. The R2 values 0.818/0.884 are present in results/records/j8_water_verdict.json but omitted from this doc's fitted-cost-model table, which does carry an R2 column in the analogous J8_SMOKE_A100.md table.

title: "batched is the faster exact baseline on all three GPUs" is falsified by the Blackwell record at B=64, and the A100 doc's "8 GB artifact" explanation was never corrected
defect: Line 88 asserts "Every qualitative feature holds on all three GPUs" and line 93 lists "batched the faster exact baseline for 3BPA at L >= 2", but this document's own device record shows serial faster than batched at every lane count at B=64 (16.32 vs 18.90, 22.12 vs 26.04, 27.92 vs 34.03, 45.31 vs 56.10 ms).
failure_scenario: J8_SMOKE_A100.md:98 states "'Batched loses to serial at B = 64' was an 8 GB memory artifact; on 80 GB batched still wins at B = 64 (81.4 vs 100.4 ms)", and the sm_120 control exists precisely to separate architecture from size. On the 102 GB Blackwell batched loses at B=64 by 24%, refuting the memory-artifact explanation - yet neither the SM120 correction section nor J8_SMOKE_A100.md carries that correction, and the SM120 doc instead lists the opposite as an invariant.

At B<=16 batched does win for L>=2, so the failure is specific to B=64.

title: The J2b L=5 CI table has no surviving record: j9a builds its output path from --score and --lanes only, so the water run clobbered the molecular run
defect: The output filename is `j9a_leading_only_ci_{score}_L{lanes}.json` and ignores `--cache-dirs`, so the water L=5 invocation overwrote the six-molecular-system L=5 record; J2B_FACTOR_B.md cites both tables but only one can exist on disk.
failure_scenario: J2B_FACTOR_B.md lines 148-153 tabulate the L=5 column (+0.021, +0.036, -0.005, +0.078, +0.060, +0.059 with CIs) for the six molecular systems, and lines 179-188 tabulate the L=5 water deltas (-0.006, -0.009, +0.582, +0.336). As shipped, results/records/j9a_leading_only_ci_global_L5.json holds only the four water rows, so the molecular L=5 column - the budget at which the ablation's headline is stated - is unreproducible from records; regenerating it silently destroys the water record the correction section depends on.

Re-running with --cache-dirs pointing at the four water caches restored the original file and values exactly. The L4 and L6 records contain the six molecular systems; only L5 was overwritten.

title: "stable rank 2.91-3.08 of 7" excludes two of the six systems it describes, whose values are 1.21 and 4.18
defect: STAGE1 line 48 and J3_EXTREME_VALUE.md line 126 quote the project's measured stable rank as "2.91-3.08 of 7", a range that comes from the frozen tree's four spectrum_*.json files, while results/records/j5_spectrum.json gives 1.212 for 3BPA overlapping and 4.175 for 3BPA same - two of the same six systems the claims cover.

J2B's later correction establishes that the sign of the leading-only advantage is controlled by exactly this variable, with the separation at srank ~ 2.5 running through the omitted values - 3BPA overlapping at 1.212 is the single molecular system where the control variate wins. Reported as 2.91-3.08 the six systems look homogeneous; measured, they span 1.21-4.18 and already contained the counterexample. Neither STAGE1 nor J3 was updated after j5_spectrum.json was written.
evidence: results/records/j5_spectrum.json stable_rank_FQ: disjoint 2.993, overlapping 1.212, same 4.175, ethanol 3.079, aspirin 2.918, azobenzene 2.908 (water 1.500-4.254). The frozen tree contains spectrum JSONs for only four systems (disjoint, ethanol, aspirin, azobenzene) = 2.908-3.079, the source of the quoted range.

title: "+0.088 to +0.230 over the best free signal" reuses the per-signal range; the best-free-signal gains are +0.067 to +0.182
defect: STAGE1:85 and J5_WATER.md:75 and :158 attach the interval +0.088 to +0.230 to the gain over the *best* free signal, but those endpoints are the min and max of the ten individual signal-by-signal comparisons in j2a_free_signal_ci.json; the gain over the best free signal per system is +0.067 to +0.182.
failure_scenario: A referee recomputing the headline from J2A_ORACLE_PANEL.md's own §3 table (gains 0.136, 0.182, 0.146, 0.067, 0.093, 0.169) finds neither endpoint of the quoted interval. The upper bound is inflated by 26%: +0.230 is the azobenzene-vs-force_norm delta, but on azobenzene the better free signal is energy_std (0.662), giving +0.169. J5_WATER.md then uses the inflated interval as the molecular reference against which water's +0.023 to +0.033 is judged "materially harsher".

title: The recommended headline "84-87% of exact evaluations avoided" is the frozen banned-split number; the journal's held-out replication gives 79-84%
defect: Both J8 documents propose "84-87% of exact evaluations avoided" as the paper's hardware-free headline, but that range comes from the frozen tree's table_gate_baselines.md (0.844/0.836/0.851/0.872), produced by scripts/07_gate_baselines.py - the file whose split implementation J1 permanently bans - while the journal's own re-run of exactly that configuration on the hashed blocked manifests gives 0.7875-0.8408.
failure_scenario: A reader looking for 84-87% in results/records/ finds nothing. j2b_factor_b_maxcomp.jsonl (control_variate, K=4, r0=2, alpha=0.05, 5 lanes - the identical configuration, since 07_gate_baselines.py defaults to score=maxcomp, r0=2, alpha=0.05) gives disjoint 0.8315, ethanol 0.8408, aspirin 0.7875, azobenzene 0.8290. Aspirin alone drops 6.4 points. The count the paper is told to lead with is therefore 3-4 points optimistic relative to the journal's own measurement, and J8_WATER_VERDICT.md:108 repeats it after J2b had already replaced it.
